text.p: The mark fought back in late Europe after an early onslaught which saw the Norwegian crown, Finnish markka and Italian lira hit their best levels in years.
Norway's crown led the way up in early Europe, making a 52-month high of 3.8955 per mark, as speculative funds continued to pour into the currency.
The markka followed suit with a leap to 2.8990 per mark -- a level not seen since September 1992 -- as its breach of its notional 2.25 percent ERM upper limit sparked panic mark sales.
Traders said medium-term investors were now entering the markka rally, with Finnish corporates buying into its strength.

"I've never seen it as aggressive as this," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London, adding that the break through 2.97, around 2.25 percent above the markka's central ERM rate of 3.04, was crucial.
"Everyone thought it would be bought back through there and it wasn't -- that's when the panic started," he said.
The markka stood at 2.9320/40 by 1513 GMT, off its earlier peak but still up from late Friday's level here of 2.9630/50.
Bank of Finland director Matti Vanhala said that the bank did not plan to cut its key tender rate soon, and that it had had a "more liberal" approach to intervention than last week.
The Norwegian crown stood at 3.9520/50 per mark by 1523 GMT, weaker than late Friday's European level of 3.9350/80 and well below its intraday high of 3.8955.
Italy's lira climbed to a 31-month peak of 966.45 during the session before slipping back to 969.70/0.05, slightly up from 970.60/1.10 late on Friday.
The market is awaiting consumer price data from key Italian cities for clues to whether the Bank of Italy might cut rates.
As for Germany, the major indicator for the market is December M3, expect this week. Economists on average foresee money supply growth slowing to 7.5 percent from 8.0 in November.
